fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. The text says, “When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully.” That's the kind of welcome where somebody grabs your bag before you can ask. Joyfully is the word the text uses.

No waiting room here, friend. Nobody leaves them standing on the porch. The text says the brothers welcomed them joyfully when they arrived. I spent years stuck in the back of a junk drawer, and this is the opposite of that.
Yes, friend. The text says that when they heard Paul's report, they glorified God. They heard what God had done and gave Him the glory. That's a good habit to bake into your own day.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a great name to reach for, friend. But the text says the believers think Paul teaches people to forsake Moses. David doesn't come up in that line. Pick the name that's in the verse and you're golden.

Exactly, friend. The elders tell Paul to take the four men, purify himself along with them and pay their expenses. Pay their expenses! That's like hearing, "You're coming with us, and you're picking up the check." The text says it's so the four can have their heads shaved.

Whoa, friend, somebody's handing out promotions! But that's not what the elders are after. They say the plan will show that there is no truth to the rumors about Paul. It's all about the rumors, and nobody mentions who is in charge.

Paul has taught plenty in other places (Acts 19:8), friend, but that's not what this verse says. He enters the temple to give notice of the date when their purification would be complete and the offering would be made for each man. Teaching the crowds isn't the errand here.
Yes, friend. The Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul at the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and seized him. That's the turn in this story. From here on, things get hard for Paul.
I wish they had, friend. A little conversation goes a long way. But the text says they stirred up the whole crowd and seized him. Asking him to explain his teaching isn't what the text records.

James and the elders are back in the earlier scene, friend, and they aren't part of this one. The text says the Jews from Asia stirred up the whole crowd and seized Paul. Reporting him to them isn't what the verse says.

Not quite, friend. The text says they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian, who traveled with Paul (Acts 20:4), with Paul in the city. Then they assumed Paul had brought him into the temple. What they saw was Trophimus in the city, and the temple part was an assumption, so this one is False.
That's right, friend. The text says that immediately he took some soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. Centurions are Roman officers. Immediately, and running, is how the text puts it.
Waiting isn't what the text says, friend. It says that immediately he took some soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. Immediately is the word it uses.
The commander goes himself, friend. He takes some soldiers and centurions and runs down to the crowd. The text says he does it immediately. A messenger isn't mentioned.

You got it, friend. After arresting Paul, the commander asks who he was and what he had done. Those are two fair questions. But the text says the commander could not get at the truth because of the uproar.
A council is a group of people, friend, and the text doesn't send Paul to one here. The commander can't get at the truth because of the uproar. So he orders Paul brought into the barracks.
Guards blocking the steps isn't in the text, friend. It says Paul had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the mob. The soldiers are the ones carrying him.
